# Results — Study 433 (Kaufman Adaptive MA) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — compute KAMA(10, 2, 30)
on daily closes, go **long when close > KAMA, flat otherwise**, enter at the next day's return
(one execution lag), NET of one-way costs × NAV turnover — and **race it head-to-head against the
identical rule on a fixed SMA(30)** and against buy-and-hold. All Sharpes are
**excess-of-cash, net, price-adjusted (`auto_adjust=True`, total-return-ish)**. As-of
**2026-05-31** (the partial June-2026 bar is dropped). Headline tape: **SPY, 1993-01-29 →
2026-05-29, n = 8,389 days**.*

## The honest test — KAMA vs fixed SMA vs buy-and-hold (SPY, long/flat, net 1 bp)

The only claim worth testing is *"the adaptive filter beats a fixed one"*, so the decisive
number is the **KAMA − SMA** daily out-performance, tested against zero with a HAC *t*.

| Book | net Sharpe | net CAGR | max DD | turnover (one-way × NAV) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Buy-and-hold | **+0.650** | +10.90% | −55.2% | 0 |
| Fixed **SMA(30)** cross | +0.530 | +5.32% | −34.8% | 765 |
| **KAMA(10,2,30)** cross | **+0.203** | +1.66% | −58.4% | 1269 |

- **KAMA loses to the fixed SMA it is supposed to improve on.** The daily KAMA − SMA
  out-performance is **−1.39 bps/day at HAC *t* = −2.98** — a *statistically significant*
  result on the **wrong** side of zero. Adapting to volatility makes the timing rule worse.
- **It also loses to buy-and-hold:** KAMA − buy-hold = **−3.88 bps/day, HAC *t* = −4.61**.
- **KAMA churns more, not less.** Despite the folk pitch of "fewer whipsaws", KAMA's
  turnover is **1269** vs the SMA's **765** — the squared smoothing constant keeps nudging
  the filter across the price even in chop, generating *extra* crossings.
- **Permutation placebo:** shuffling KAMA's daily positions and re-booking gives
  ***p* = 0.995** — the real book's mean is *worse* than almost every shuffle. There is no
  timing information to harvest; the signal is anti-informative net of costs.

## Panel — five of six tapes say the adaptation hurts (long/flat, net 1 bp)

| Ticker | KAMA Sharpe | SMA Sharpe | buy-hold | KAMA − SMA HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | +0.203 | +0.530 | +0.650 | **−2.98** |
| QQQ  | +0.181 | +0.521 | +0.523 | **−2.79** |
| IWM  | −0.089 | +0.243 | +0.472 | **−2.86** |
| EFA  | +0.168 | +0.421 | +0.406 | **−2.23** |
| GLD  | +0.464 | +0.436 | +0.666 | +0.07 |
| AAPL | +0.579 | +0.766 | +0.628 | **−2.49** |

Only GLD ties (*t* = +0.07); on every equity tape the adaptive filter is *significantly*
behind the plain SMA, and **no tape clears the +2 bar** for "KAMA beats SMA".

## Cost sweep (SPY, KAMA − SMA) — costs *widen* the gap

| round-trip cost | KAMA Sharpe | SMA Sharpe | KAMA − SMA (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bp (gross) | +0.237 | +0.551 | −1.327 | −2.87 |
| 0.5 bp | +0.220 | +0.540 | −1.357 | −2.92 |
| 1.0 bp | +0.203 | +0.530 | −1.387 | −2.98 |
| 2.0 bp | +0.169 | +0.509 | −1.447 | −3.09 |
| 5.0 bp | +0.067 | +0.445 | −1.627 | −3.41 |

The gap is already negative **gross**; KAMA's higher turnover means costs make it *worse*,
not better — the opposite of the whipsaw-avoidance pitch.

## Robustness (SPY, net 1 bp) — the sign never flips

| Variant | KAMA Sharpe | SMA Sharpe | KAMA − SMA HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| slow=20 / SMA(20) | +0.178 | +0.415 | −2.68 |
| slow=30 / SMA(30) | +0.203 | +0.530 | −2.98 |
| slow=50 / SMA(50) | +0.200 | +0.488 | −2.42 |
| ER period = 5 | +0.149 | +0.530 | −2.83 |
| ER period = 20 | +0.388 | +0.530 | −1.76 |
| **Long/short** | −0.411 | −0.032 | −3.01 |

The longer ER window (20) narrows the gap but never makes KAMA win; the long/short
variant is a disaster (−0.41 Sharpe vs −0.03 for SMA L/S, both far below buy-and-hold).

## Synthetic positive control — the harness *can* find a KAMA edge when one is planted

On the deterministic [`data.synthetic_panel`](../kama_adaptive/data.py) — strong clean trend
blocks (efficiency ≈ 1) alternating with whippy near-zero chop blocks (efficiency ≈ 0),
at a realistic **2 bp** cost — the same engine recovers a *positive* KAMA − SMA edge once
the trend/chop contrast is strong enough:

| Planted edge | KAMA Sharpe | SMA Sharpe | KAMA − SMA HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 (random walk) | +0.100 | +0.008 | +0.81 (null) |
| 2.0 | +3.658 | +4.036 | −3.38 |
| 4.0 | +6.881 | +6.795 | +1.15 |
| **8.0** | +9.589 | +9.180 | **+2.86** |

At ``edge = 0`` the difference is noise; at a strong planted edge KAMA's whipsaw avoidance
finally beats the SMA at *t* = +2.86. The engine is faithful — **the real market simply
isn't the regime-switching tape KAMA needs**, and on real SPY the sign is the *opposite*.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** KAMA − SMA daily out-performance is **−1.39 bps/day, HAC *t* = −2.98**
  on SPY (significantly *negative*), five of six tapes significantly behind the plain SMA,
  permutation *p* = 0.995. KAMA carries no timing edge over a fixed SMA — it carries a
  reliable *dis*advantage. *(Caveat: the basket is surviving liquid ETFs/large-caps; the
  bias works toward holding being good, which is exactly what beats both filters here.)*
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Both filters lose to buy-and-hold (KAMA Sharpe +0.20, SMA +0.53,
  buy-hold +0.65), and KAMA's higher turnover means costs deepen its loss. Nothing to deploy.
- **"Adapting to volatility beats a fixed SMA?" — BUSTED.** The adaptation makes the rule
  *worse* (significantly so) and *raises* turnover — the exact reverse of the marketing.
